1233.title: Spiritual friendship
1233.hook: Aelred of Rievaulx wrote that God is friendship
1233.howItsDone: Christians often seek friends who share their faith: prayer partners, small groups, sponsors and godparents, and in some traditions a spiritual director; monastic communities treat friendship as part of the life of prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, open doors: Abraham running to meet three strangers, and an ordinary kitchen table. Your line was an open door.

An English abbot named Aelred sits down to talk with a younger monk about friendship. He wrote the conversation up as a book, and it reads like a real talk between two people who trust each other. The abbot opens it gently. Here we are, he says, you and I, and he hopes a third is with them: Christ, in the middle. A little later the young monk asks a startling question. Scripture says God is love. Could we say God is friendship? The abbot doesn't laugh him off.

The line the monk is reaching for is in the first letter of John: "God is love; and he that dwelleth in love dwelleth in God, and God in him." Aelred's answer, as he tells it, is honest. Saying God is friendship is unusual, and scripture doesn't say it. But what is true of love, he will not hesitate to say of friendship. Whoever lives in friendship lives in God. So Aelred is careful about which friendship he means. He describes friendships built on pleasure, and friendships built on what someone can do for you. Those come and go. Spiritual friendship is different: two people who want the good for each other, and who help each other toward God. The Bible has its own pictures of that kind of friendship. Jonathan and David: "the soul of Jonathan was knit with the soul of David, and Jonathan loved him as his own soul." Proverbs: "Iron sharpeneth iron; so a man sharpeneth the countenance of his friend." And at the last supper, in a line this path heard on day six hundred thirty-five, Jesus says it himself: "Henceforth I call you not servants; for the servant knoweth not what his lord doeth: but I have called you friends." In Christian life this shows up in plain ways. A prayer partner. Monks and nuns in community. A small group that knows when you're struggling. Some churches name the role: a spiritual director, a sponsor, a godparent. What Aelred adds is the third person at the table. A friendship like that has room for one more.

Let one person come to mind who has helped you toward what's good: a friend who told you the truth when it stung, someone who just kept showing up. Go back to one moment with them, and let a short, plain thank-you form in your head. If you pray, you can give thanks to God for them by name.
Spiritual friendship. In Aelred's picture, a friendship with Christ as the third in the room: two people who want the good for each other and help each other toward God.
Your line: friendship is holy. Two friends, and Christ in the middle. See you tomorrow.

1234.title: In everything give thanks (1 Thessalonians 5:18)
1234.howItsDone: Christians practice gratitude through grace before meals, thanksgiving at the start of prayer, and some through a nightly review of the day's gifts; churches give thanks in worship together, and some keep special days of thanksgiving.

segments.voice: Yesterday, spiritual friendship: Aelred and the third one in the room. Your line was friendship is holy.

"Rejoice evermore. Pray without ceasing. In every thing give thanks." Three short lines near the end of Paul's first letter to the Thessalonians. On a coffee mug they'd look cheerful, almost easy. Then read the letter around them. Paul says this church received the word "in much affliction." He writes to comfort them about friends who have died, those he calls "them which are asleep." These are people in trouble and in grief. And to them, not to people having a good week, he writes: in every thing, give thanks.

The King James reads: "In every thing give thanks: for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you." In every thing. Some readers lean hard on that little word. On their reading, Paul doesn't ask the grieving to be thankful that their friends died. He asks them to find thanks inside whatever is happening. Other readers point to Ephesians, which says "giving thanks always for all things," and hold the two lines together. Either way, the thanks doesn't wait for the trouble to clear. Paul seems to have practiced it himself. Writing to the Philippians while in bonds, he says: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content." Learned. Something practiced, not something he was born with. And there's an older pattern behind him. Psalm 136 repeats one refrain, line after line: "for his mercy endureth for ever." Thanks as a rhythm, said again and again until it sinks in. One more example. On the night Jesus was betrayed, Luke says, "he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it." Thanks, at that table, on that night. Christians build this into ordinary days. A grace said before a meal. A few minutes at bedtime looking back for the day's gifts. A line of thanks at the start of prayer, before any asking. Not a feeling summoned on command. A habit of looking.

Count ten gifts on your fingers, small and specific: not my family, but the way your sister laughed on the phone; not health, but the knee that worked on the stairs this morning. If the day has been hard, look inside it anyway, the way Paul asked, and if you pray, say thanks for each one. If grief feels too heavy to carry alone, or you're thinking of harming yourself, please call or text 988 in the US, or reach local emergency help.
In everything give thanks. Paul's line to a grieving church: thanks found inside every situation, not saved for the good days.
Your line: in everything, thanks. The thanks doesn't wait for the trouble to clear. Until tomorrow.

1235.title: Holy laughter
1235.hook: saints often laughed; joy is a fruit of the Spirit
1235.tomorrow: Block close: the shape of a life
1235.howItsDone: Christians count joy among the fruit of the Spirit; laughter and celebration are part of church life at weddings, baptisms, feasts and fellowship meals, and some traditions tell stories of saints known for their humor.

segments.voice: Yesterday, in everything give thanks: Paul writing to a grieving church. Your line was in everything, thanks.

Three days ago on this path, Abraham was running to feed three strangers at his tent. Today, stay inside with Sarah, listening behind the door. Outside, one of the visitors is saying that Sarah will have a son. Genesis is blunt about it: Abraham and Sarah "were old and well stricken in age." So Sarah does the obvious thing. "Sarah laughed within herself." Quietly. To herself. And the visitor hears it anyway. "Wherefore did Sarah laugh?" She is afraid. "I laughed not." And the answer comes back, almost gently: "Nay; but thou didst laugh." A whole family story in Genesis turns on a laugh.

That first laugh is a hidden one, a laugh of disbelief. Then the promise comes true, and Sarah laughs again, this time out loud and on purpose: "God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me." The boy is named Isaac, and readers of the Hebrew hear laughter in the name, as this path did on day three hundred fifty-five. The story moves from a laugh behind a door to a laugh the whole neighborhood is invited to share. The Bible keeps a place for that second kind. Ecclesiastes says there is "a time to weep, and a time to laugh." A psalm about coming home from exile says: "Then was our mouth filled with laughter, and our tongue with singing." And Jesus, in Luke, makes it a promise: "Blessed are ye that weep now: for ye shall laugh." Paul names joy as part of what grows in a life where God is at work: "the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace." Joy, in second place. And Christian memory keeps laughing saints. Tradition says that Lawrence, a deacon of Rome, was put to death on a gridiron and joked with his executioners: turn me over, this side is done. Orthodox Christians honor holy fools, who took Paul's words "we are fools for Christ's sake" at face value. None of this laughs at faith. It's laughter that comes from it. Solemn and holy aren't the same word.
screen: `ALL THAT HEAR WILL LAUGH WITH ME.`
`THE FRUIT OF THE SPIRIT IS JOY.`

segments.voice: Bring back a time you laughed until it hurt: who was there, what set it off, the room, the faces, the moment it tipped over. If a smile comes, let it, and if a real laugh comes, let that come too; nobody's grading this. If you pray, you can give thanks for the joy, and for the people you laughed with.
Holy laughter. Joy that comes from faith, not at its expense: Sarah's laugh shared with everyone who hears, and joy named among the fruit of the Spirit.
Your line: joy is holy. Laughter can come from faith, not at its expense. Rest well.

1236.title: Block close: the shape of a life
1236.hook: commandments, virtues and mercy, gathered up in love
1236.howItsDone: Churches teach Jesus's two great commandments, love of God and love of neighbor, as a summary of Christian ethics, and teach the commandments and virtues as ways that love takes shape in daily life.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sarah's laugh, first behind the door, then shared. Your line was joy is holy.

An expert in the law steps forward with a test question for Jesus. In Matthew he asks: "Master, which is the great commandment in the law?" The law is long, and a person could spend a lifetime arguing about which part matters most. Jesus gives him two, and then says something that gathers everything up. This block of the path has walked through Christian ethics: commandments, virtues, mercy, money, peace, the poor, the stranger, enemies, friends. Today, one last question: what holds all of that together?

Jesus answers: "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind. This is the first and great commandment. And the second is like unto it, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself. On these two commandments hang all the law and the prophets." Both lines come from the Torah, Deuteronomy and Leviticus. The first belongs to the Shema, the passage that opens with Hear, O Israel. Jesus doesn't invent a new law here; he names what the law hangs on, like a coat on a hook. Paul says it his own way. In Romans he lists commandments, do not kill, do not steal, do not covet, and says they are "briefly comprehended in this saying, namely, Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Then: "Love worketh no ill to his neighbour: therefore love is the fulfilling of the law." Fulfilling, not canceling. Love doesn't make the commandments optional. It's what they were reaching for all along. Colossians adds a picture. After a list of virtues, kindness, humility, patience, forgiveness, it says: "And above all these things put on charity, which is the bond of perfectness." Love as the belt that holds the rest in place. Augustine, in a sermon on the first letter of John, pushed it into a short line, remembered in English as: love, and do what you will. He meant a love that sometimes says no, the way a parent does. So here is the shape of a life, as this block has traced it: Commandments as the frame. Virtues as the habits. Mercy, peace and welcome as the practice. And love underneath all of it.
screen: `LOVE IS THE FULFILLING OF THE LAW.`

segments.voice: Ask what three short, plain lines could give this year its shape: call my mother on Sundays, give before I spend, say the hard thing kindly. Let each one be a form of love, toward God if you pray, toward a neighbor, and turn them over until they're short enough to remember.
Block close. The end of this block on Christian ethics: commandments, virtues and mercy, gathered up in love, which Paul calls the fulfilling of the law.
Your line: love fulfils it all. Tomorrow a new block begins: the great thinkers. That closes this block.

1237.title: Seeds of the Word
1237.hook: Justin Martyr said wisdom in pagan philosophers came from seeds of the Word
1237.howItsDone: Christian teachers since Justin have drawn on Greek philosophy to explain the faith; churches differ on how much truth they find in other philosophies and religions, and some Catholic teaching uses Justin's phrase "seeds of the Word".

segments.voice: Yesterday, the block close, all of it gathered up in love. Your line was love fulfils it all.

A young man is shopping for a philosophy. One teacher wants to talk about fees before truth. Another tells him to master music and geometry first. He settles on the Platonists, until one day, walking alone near the sea, he meets an old man who starts asking him questions he can't answer. The old man points him to the prophets and to Christ, then walks off. A fire, he says later, was kindled in his soul. That's how Justin tells his own story. A new block starts today, the great thinkers, and Justin goes first.

Justin became a Christian, but he didn't throw away his philosopher's books. He kept a question: what about all the true things Plato and the others said? His answer starts with the opening of John's Gospel: "In the beginning was the Word." In Greek, the Word is the Logos. And John says of it: "That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world." So Justin reasoned that the Word had been sowing seeds long before anyone heard of Jesus. In a defense addressed to the Roman authorities, he writes, roughly, that whatever has been rightly said among all people belongs to us Christians, and that the writers of the past saw truly by the seed of the Word planted in them. He thought they saw in part, and that in Jesus the whole Word had come. But he would not call their wisdom worthless. There was a precedent, in the same speech at Athens this path heard two weeks ago. There Paul quotes Greek poets to the crowd: "For in him we live, and move, and have our being; as certain also of your own poets have said, For we are also his offspring." Justin paid for his faith. Tradition says he died for it in Rome, which is why he's remembered as Justin Martyr. Christians still weigh his idea differently. Some find seeds of truth widely scattered. Others stress more sharply what only Christ reveals. This path ranks neither. Justin's question can travel with anyone: when you hear something true, where did the seed come from?

Bring to mind a person whose life looks very different from yours: different politics, a different faith or none, a different generation. Look for one wise thing they've said or done, and without arguing with the rest of what they think, hold that one thing and turn it over, the way Justin read Plato. If you pray, you can give thanks for the wisdom, wherever it came from.
Seeds of the Word. Justin's idea that the Word of God sows truth in people everywhere, so wisdom found anywhere can be honored.
Your line: seeds everywhere. Wisdom found anywhere, by anyone, can be honored. See you tomorrow.

1238.title: Irenaeus against contempt for matter
1238.hook: against those who called the world evil, he defended bodies and creation
1238.howItsDone: Christians confess God as maker of heaven and earth and the resurrection of the body in their creeds; churches honor the body through sacraments that use water, bread, wine and oil, through care for the sick, and through Christian burial.

segments.voice: Yesterday, seeds of the Word: Justin finding truth sown in the philosophers. Your line was seeds everywhere.

An aching back. Bad news on the phone. Someone you love, sick. For some teachers in the early church, there was a tidy explanation for all of it: the world itself was the mistake. Matter was a trap, built by a lesser power, and the body was a cage. Salvation meant secret knowledge, and the secret was how to get out. Later writers group these teachers under the name Gnostic, though they did not all agree. A bishop in Lyon, in Gaul, thought they had it exactly backward. His name was Irenaeus, and he wrote a long work called Against Heresies.

Irenaeus starts where the Bible starts. Genesis closes the sixth day with a verdict: "And God saw every thing that he had made, and, behold, it was very good." Not a mistake. Very good. Rocks, rivers, animals, bodies. Then he points to the center of the faith: "And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us." If flesh were a cage, why would God's own Word step into it? Then the table. Bread comes from the earth and wine from the vine, and in the Eucharist, he argues, these ordinary things receive the word of God and become the gift of Christ's body and blood. If wheat and grapes can carry that, how can anyone say the flesh is worthless? And forward, to the resurrection. The Apostles' Creed confesses the resurrection of the body: not a soul set loose, but a body raised. For Irenaeus, the whole story is God making, and then God mending what was made, not God throwing it away. He sums it up in a line, here in paraphrase: the glory of God is a human being fully alive, and human life is seeing God. Paul says something close: "know ye not that your body is the temple of the Holy Ghost which is in you?" A temple, not a cage. Some churches draw on this when they care for the sick, bless fields and gardens, and bury their dead with care. Bodies matter. Bread matters. The ground under your feet matters.

Start at your feet and move slowly up, legs, back, hands, shoulders, face, noticing without judging where you're tired and where you're carrying something. Then pick one small act of care for today: a glass of water, a walk around the block, an early night. If you pray, you can give thanks for your body, the one Genesis would call very good.
Irenaeus against contempt for matter. A bishop defending creation and the body as God's good work, against teachers who called the world a trap.

1239.title: Origen's search
1239.hook: a brilliant, controversial teacher who read scripture as a journey upward
1239.howItsDone: Christians read scripture for its plain sense and for deeper meanings; spiritual reading such as lectio divina moves slowly from what a text says to what it asks and to prayer, and preachers draw out both history and meaning.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Irenaeus: creation called very good, and bread from the earth. Your line was matter matters.

Read the first chapter of Genesis slowly and something odd turns up. "And the evening and the morning were the first day." Then a second day. Then a third. Evenings and mornings, one after another. And only on the fourth day does God make the sun. In Alexandria, a teacher named Origen noticed exactly this, and pointed it out to his readers. He didn't close the book. He didn't pretend not to see it. He took it as a signal: keep going, there's more here than the surface.

Origen gave his students a picture. A human being, he said, is body, soul and spirit, and so is scripture. Paul uses those three words together: "your whole spirit and soul and body." The body of scripture is its plain sense, the story as it stands, and Origen held that it feeds many readers well. The soul is what the text asks of your life. The spirit is where it points: toward Christ and toward God. So reading becomes a climb, from the words, through your life, up toward God. He leaned on Paul again: "the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life." He was brilliant, and he was controversial, then and later. Some of his bolder guesses, about where souls come from and how all things end, were condemned long after he died. Others honor him as a giant of Christian learning. Christians still argue about how to read him, and this path won't settle it. Tradition says he suffered in a persecution for his faith. Here's his search on the road. In Luke, two disciples walk to Emmaus with a stranger who opens the scriptures to them. Only later do they recognize the risen Jesus. Afterward they say: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" That's reading upward. And look back at this week's road. A friend as the third in the room. Thanks in every thing. A holy laugh. Love gathering up the law. Seeds of truth. Matter that matters. And now a search that keeps climbing.
screen: `THE LETTER KILLETH, THE SPIRIT GIVETH LIFE.`

segments.voice: Take one line from the Psalms, "The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want," and give each layer a few breaths: what does it say, a shepherd, a sheep, enough; what does it ask of your life today, maybe to stop grabbing; and where does it point? Let it lead you upward as far as it will go, and if you pray, rest in the line itself.
Origen's search. A teacher who read scripture as a climb, from its plain sense, through the life of the reader, up toward God.
Your line: read upward. From the words, through your life, up toward God. That closes the week.
